extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (and patent practitioners advising on examination/prosecution)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for interpreting patent claims during USPTO examination, including rules for broadest reasonable interpretation, plain meaning, importing limitations, means-plus-function, preamble effect, and joint inventorship contribution rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantum of collaboration for joint inventorship
rubrics_metrics.description: For persons to be joint inventors under Section 116, there must be some element of joint behavior, such as collaboration or working under common direction, one inventor seeing a relevant report and building upon it or hearing another’s suggestion at a meeting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some 'quantum of collaboration or connection' is required; inventors may be unaware of each other's work but joint inventorship requires some element of collaboration or connection. (Kimberly-Clark Corp. v. Procter & Gamble; Moler v. Purdy.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Each joint inventor must contribute to conception (type/amount may differ)
rubrics_metrics.description: While each joint inventor must generally contribute to the conception of the invention, each joint inventor does not have to 'make the same type or amount of contribution' to the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different roles and unequal contributions are permissible; a partial original contribution by each that helps reach the final solution is sufficient. (Monsanto Co. v. Kamp.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Contribution to a single claim suffices for joint inventorship
rubrics_metrics.description: A joint inventor or coinventor need not make a contribution to every claim of a patent; a contribution to one claim is enough.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The contributor of any disclosed means of a means-plus-function claim element is a joint inventor as to that claim unless the contribution was only a reduction to practice of the sole inventor’s broader concept. There is no requirement that all inventors be joint inventors of the subject matter of any one claim. (Ethicon Inc. v. United States Surgical Corp.) See MPEP § 602.09 and § 602.01(c) et seq. for correction of inventorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must be given their broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) in light of the specification
rubrics_metrics.description: During patent examination, the pending claims must be 'given their broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The PTO determines claim scope not solely on claim language but by giving claims their broadest reasonable construction as would be interpreted by one of ordinary skill in the art, taking into account the specification. BRI is applied during prosecution (not in court) because applicants can amend claims; BRI reduces the possibility claims later issue with wider-than-justified scope. BRI is not the broadest possible interpretation — it must be consistent with ordinary/customary meaning and the specification. (Phillips; In re Am. Acad. of Sci. Tech. Ctr.; In re Yamamoto; In re Zletz, et al.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Words of a claim must be given their plain meaning unless inconsistent with the specification
rubrics_metrics.description: Under BRI, words of the claim must be given their plain meaning, unless such meaning is inconsistent with the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plain meaning = ordinary and customary meaning given by those of ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention; best sources include the claims themselves, the specification, drawings, and prior art. The specification is the best source when it serves as a glossary. Applicant can rebut the presumption by clearly setting forth a different definition in the specification. Examples and case law illustrate when plain meaning applies or is rebutted (Morris; In re Zletz; Chef America; etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not import limitations from the specification into the claims
rubrics_metrics.description: It is improper to import into a claim limitations that are not part of the claim simply because they appear in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A particular embodiment in the written description may not be read into a claim when the claim language is broader than the embodiment. Examiners should avoid importing unrecited limitations from the specification into claims. When 112(f) means-plus-function language is used, the specification must be consulted to determine corresponding structure/material/acts. (Superguide; Liebel-Flarsheim; E-Pass; In re Donaldson; In re Marosi; In re Okuzawa.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Means-plus-function (35 U.S.C. 112(f)) elements are limited to corresponding structure/material/acts in the specification and equivalents
rubrics_metrics.description: When an element is claimed using means- (or step-) plus-function language, the specification must be consulted to determine the structure, material, or acts corresponding to the function recited in the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The claimed element is construed as limited to the corresponding structure, material, or acts described in the specification and equivalents thereof. Cite In re Donaldson and MPEP § 2181–2186.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordinary and customary meaning determined from specification, drawings, claims, and prior art; extrinsic evidence rarely needed when specification is clear
rubrics_metrics.description: The ordinary and customary meaning of a term is the meaning that the term would have to a person of ordinary skill in the art as of the effective filing date; it may be evidenced by claims, specification, drawings, and prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the specification is clear about scope and content of a claim term, there is no need to turn to extrinsic evidence. Prior art usage must be consistent with specification. Case law (e.g., 3M; In re Suitco Surface; Vitronics; In re Abbott Diabetes Care) supports relying on the specification where clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant may act as lexicographer (special definitions in the specification)
rubrics_metrics.description: The applicant may rebut the presumption of ordinary meaning by clearly setting forth a special definition of a claim term in the specification that differs from its ordinary meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Special definitions must be provided 'with reasonable clarity, deliberateness, and precision' and set out in the patent disclosure so one of ordinary skill is on notice of the change. Where an explicit definition is provided, that definition will control. (In re Paulsen; Intellicall; Toro Co.; Old Town Canoe; Multiform Desiccants; MPEP § 2173.05(a)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant may disavow or disclaim claim scope only by clear and unmistakable statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicant may rebut plain meaning by clearly disavowing the full scope of a claim term in the specification, but disavowal must be 'clear and unmistakable.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disavowal may be express or in some cases implied (e.g., repeated, consistent depiction with disparaging remarks about alternatives). If examiner believes implicit disavowal narrows BRI, the examiner should make the interpretation clear on the record. (SciMed; In re Am. Acad. of Sci. Tech Ctr.; In re Abbott Diabetes Care.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner decision flow for determining meaning of claim term not invoking 35 U.S.C. 112(f)
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow a decision flow: determine whether a claim term has an ordinary and customary meaning to those of ordinary skill; if yes, check whether the specification provides a special definition; if no special definition, apply ordinary meaning; if special definition exists, use it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a claim term does not have an ordinary and customary meaning, examiner should check the specification for a meaning. If no reasonably clear meaning emerges from specification and prior art, apply the broadest reasonable interpretation and reject the claim under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) and object to the specification under 37 CFR 1.75(d). If the specification provides a meaning, the examiner should use that meaning and may acknowledge/identify the special definition in the Office action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of preamble is determined case-by-case; preamble may be limiting or not
rubrics_metrics.description: The determination of whether a preamble limits a claim is made on a case-by-case basis in light of the facts in each case; there is no litmus test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the preamble, read in context of the entire claim, recites limitations or is 'necessary to give life, meaning, and vitality' to the claim, then it should be treated as a limitation. If the claim body fully sets forth all limitations and the preamble merely states purpose or intended use, it is not a limitation. Examiners must evaluate whether preamble recitations of purpose or intended use result in a structural (or manipulative for process claims) difference from the prior art; if so, the preamble limits. Case examples: Catalina Marketing; Bell Communications Research; Pitney Bowes; Corning Glass; Jansen; Rowe; STX; In re Otto; In re Sinex; In re Schreiber; In re Cruciferous Sprout Litig.
